props.title: Silent Souls

sections.content: **Silent Souls (2010)** (2010) stands as a haunting meditation on grief, ritual, and cultural memory in post-Soviet Russia. Director Aleksei Fedorchenko crafts a mesmerizing road movie that follows two men as they journey to cremate a beloved wife according to ancient Meryan traditions. The film's approach echoes the measured patience of **The Sweet Hereafter** (1997) and carries the spiritual weight of **Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner** (2001), particularly in how it preserves disappearing indigenous customs through cinema. The stunning cinematography by Mikhail Krichman (who also shot **Leviathan** (2014)) transforms the Russian wilderness into a character itself.

sections.content: This film belongs to a vital wave of contemporary Russian cinema that explores loss and identity in the post-Soviet landscape. Like **Elena** (2011) and **Leviathan** (2014), it examines how ancient traditions collide with modern life. The careful attention to Meryan rituals recalls how **Ixcanul** (2015) preserved Mayan customs through its narrative, though Fedorchenko's approach is more elegiac, letting silence and landscape speak volumes about cultural extinction.

The film's visual poetry shares DNA with other great Eastern European works about memory and tradition, particularly The Turin Horse (2011) and **On Body and Soul** (2017). Its use of water imagery and its themes of ritual purification connect it to **Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring** (2003), though Fedorchenko's approach is distinctly Russian in its stark beauty and emotional restraint. sections.content: Like **Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives** (2010), Silent Souls weaves together memory, ritual and landscape into a meditation on disappearing worlds. The film's focus on the Meryan people's customs mirrors how **Embrace of the Serpent** (2015) documented vanishing Amazonian traditions, though Fedorchenko's approach is more intimate, focusing on personal grief rather than colonial destruction.
